subsection: 1. Alternating governments and their economic and social policies, 1948–1959

notes.b: A coalition of Fine Gael, Labour, Clann na Poblachta, Clann na Talmhan and the National Labour Party ended 16 years of Fianna Fáil rule in February 1948.
points: Taoiseach John A. Costello led the government; Seán MacBride of Clann na Poblachta was Minister for External Affairs.
The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 came into force on 18 April 1949, when the state formally left the Commonwealth and became a republic.
The Ireland Act 1949 (UK) stated that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of its parliament, which the Republic had made a central grievance.
The Industrial Development Authority (IDA) was set up in 1949 to attract foreign manufacturing investment and to promote industrial grants.
Ireland received Marshall Aid from 1948 under the European Recovery Programme, which supported reconstruction after the Second World War.
Noël Browne, as Minister for Health, ran a campaign against tuberculosis, which had a high death rate in the late 1940s, using sanatoria and the BCG vaccine programme.

notes.h: The Mother and Child Scheme crisis, 1950–1951
notes.b: The scheme was the most public clash between the state and the Catholic Church in this period.
points: Browne proposed free GP care for mothers and children under 16, with free hospital care for mothers, as a measure to lower infant and maternal mortality.

Archbishop John Charles McQuaid of Dublin and the Catholic hierarchy objected that the scheme extended state control into family life and bypassed the role of the family and the church in health care.
Doctors' representatives, including the Irish Medical Association, opposed the scheme's effect on their independent practice.
Costello's cabinet withdrew its support for the scheme, and Browne resigned in April 1951.
The affair showed that the Catholic hierarchy could block social legislation it regarded as contrary to Catholic teaching, a point later historians cite for church influence in the 1950s.
Éamon de Valera returned as Taoiseach after the 1951 general election, with Seán MacEntee as Minister for Finance.
MacEntee's 1952 budget was deflationary: it raised taxes and cut spending to reduce the state's borrowing and imports.
The budget was unpopular, and Fianna Fáil lost its overall majority in the 1954 general election.
Unemployment and emigration continued to rise through the early 1950s, with the population falling as young people left.

notes.b: Costello returned as Taoiseach in 1954 at the head of a coalition that lacked a clear programme for economic growth.
points: Gerard Sweetman, Minister for Finance, presented budgets that raised taxes and cut current spending to deal with the balance of payments deficit.
The 1955–1956 balance of payments crisis came from imports exceeding exports, with a shortfall of foreign currency reserves that the state had to cover.
The Capital Investment Advisory Committee was set up in 1956 to examine public investment proposals and to control spending on capital projects.
Sweetman's 1956 budget increased taxation sharply, which hit working families and the farming community.
The government fell in 1957 after a general election in which voters gave Fianna Fáil back power.

notes.h: Stagnation, unemployment and emigration in the 1950s
notes.b: The decade is often described as the wasted years because growth was slow and many people left the country.
points: Population fell from about 2.96 million in 1951 to about 2.8 million by 1961 (about, verify before use).
The 1950s saw large-scale net emigration, with about 400,000 people leaving the country over the decade, a figure often cited (verify).
Most emigrants were young and went to Britain, which offered jobs in construction, manufacturing and nursing.
Agriculture was the main economic activity, and the rural economy relied on small farms with low productivity.

Industrial output grew slowly, and most manufacturing was protected behind tariffs under the Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 (see the notes on the First Programme for Economic Expansion).
Historians describe the 1950s as the wasted years, a term in use from the late 1950s, to criticise governments for failing to plan economic growth.

notes.h: Fianna Fáil's return and the debate over the 1950s
points: Fianna Fáil won the 1957 general election and de Valera returned as Taoiseach, with Seán Lemass as Tánaiste and Minister for Industry and Commerce.
Supporters of the Inter-Party governments argue that they laid groundwork for later growth through the IDA and Marshall Aid.
Critics argue that the coalitions reacted to balance of payments crises with deflation, instead of planning investment for growth.
Historians disagree on whether the wasted years were caused mainly by government policy, by the limits of an open economy dependent on Britain, or by a combination of both.
Achievements: the Republic of Ireland Act completed the break with the Commonwealth; the IDA and Marshall Aid laid foundations for later industrial growth.
Limits: no government in the decade produced a long-term plan, and the balance of payments repeatedly forced deflationary budgets.
Contemporary view: many voters blamed the coalitions for emigration and high taxes, which helped bring Fianna Fáil back in 1957.
Later view: historians see the decade as a period of economic stagnation that was made worse by policy choices, but they also credit it with ending the isolation of the 1930s and 1940s.

keyTerms.definition: The record of a country's trade and financial flows with the rest of the world; a deficit means more money leaves the country than comes in, forcing deflation or borrowing.
Government policy that raises taxes and cuts spending to reduce demand, imports and borrowing, at the cost of lower output and jobs.
Noël Browne's 1950 proposal for free maternity and child health care, withdrawn in 1951 after opposition from the Catholic hierarchy and the medical profession.
American aid under the European Recovery Programme, paid to Ireland from 1948 to help rebuild the economy after the Second World War.
The state body set up in 1949 to attract foreign manufacturing investment and to offer grants to new industry.
The term used for the 1950s, describing slow growth, high unemployment and mass emigration that historians attribute partly to the lack of economic planning.
The 1948 act, in force from 18 April 1949, that declared the state a republic and ended its membership of the Commonwealth.

factCards.term: First Inter-Party Government: Taoiseach and key minister
factCards.definition: John A. Costello was Taoiseach; Seán MacBride of Clann na Poblachta was Minister for External Affairs and the most prominent republican in the coalition.

factCards.term: Date the Republic of Ireland Act took effect
factCards.definition: The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 came into force on 18 April 1949.

factCards.term: The Ireland Act 1949 and Northern Ireland
factCards.definition: The UK's Ireland Act 1949 said Northern Ireland would remain part of the UK unless its parliament consented to a change.
Browne was Minister for Health in the First Inter-Party Government and proposed the Mother and Child Scheme.

factCards.term: Who opposed the Mother and Child Scheme
factCards.definition: The Catholic hierarchy, led by Archbishop McQuaid, and the medical profession, through the Irish Medical Association, opposed the scheme.

factCards.term: Year Browne resigned over the Mother and Child Scheme
factCards.definition: Browne resigned from government in April 1951 after his cabinet colleagues withdrew support for the scheme.
Seán MacEntee's deflationary budget of 1952 raised taxes and cut spending to deal with the balance of payments deficit.
Sweetman was Minister for Finance in the Second Inter-Party Government and presented tax-raising budgets in 1955 and 1956.

factCards.term: Year of the Capital Investment Advisory Committee
factCards.definition: The Capital Investment Advisory Committee was set up in 1956 to vet public capital spending.
The 1951 census recorded a population of about 2.96 million, the lowest level of the twentieth century up to that point (about, verify).
About 400,000 people are estimated to have left the state during the 1950s, mostly for Britain (about, verify).

factCards.term: Year of Fianna Fáil's return to power
factCards.definition: Fianna Fáil returned to government in 1957 after the general election of that year, with de Valera again as Taoiseach.
